descs.t: France is urging curfews in some areas after a weekend of riots, and Paris police have ordered an overnight curfew in 2 areas of the capital. Reuters, AP and Politico report that President Macron has rejected his interior minister's resignation. We walk through where the curfews apply, what the government is weighing next, and what it says about the state of the country.

The France riots have turned into a test of Emmanuel Macron's final months in office, with curfews in French cities and a ban on gatherings under consideration. Reuters calls the unrest a sign of the slow agony of his twilight months, while Marine Le Pen vows war on the rioters. We look at what this means for Macron, for Le Pen, and for who controls France's streets.

France is burning, curfews are back, and Macron is weighing a ban on gatherings while Marine Le Pen vows war on the rioters. In some towns shopkeepers and locals fought back against the looters themselves. We break down why the state struggled, why ordinary people stepped in, and why these riots may be the final chapter of Macron's presidency.

intro.plain: France is putting curfews on parts of the country after a weekend of riots. Paris police ordered an overnight curfew in two areas of the capital, and Macron refused his interior minister's resignation. So the government is staying put and tightening up. Chat, here is my question: do curfews actually stop riots like this, or just push them to another night?
intro.mid: This weekend's riots in France are turning into a verdict on Macron himself. Curfews in several cities, a ban on gatherings on the table, his interior minister offering to resign and Macron saying no. Reuters is already calling these his twilight months. Chat, tell me: is this the moment Macron's presidency effectively ended?
intro.bold: France burned this weekend, and the people who stopped it in some towns were not the police. They were shopkeepers and locals fighting off looters. Now Macron wants curfews and maybe a ban on gatherings, and Le Pen is vowing war on the rioters. Chat, straight question: when citizens have to defend their own shops, has the state already failed?

hook.plain: Paris police just ordered an overnight curfew in two parts of the capital. Here is how a weekend of riots got France to this point, and what comes after.
hook.mid: Macron's own interior minister offered to quit over these riots, and Macron said no. Here is why this weekend could define the end of his presidency.
hook.bold: In parts of France, shopkeepers had to fight off the looters themselves. Here is how the state lost the streets, and who is promising to take them back.

descs.t: Israel is resuming commercial shipments and private sector goods into Gaza after a dispute over fees involving Hamas, Reuters and The Times of Israel report. The move comes as 5 people were reportedly killed in the Strip and the World Food Programme says it is cutting aid to 500,000 Palestinians over funding shortages. We walk through what the fee dispute was, what changes now, and what it means for Gaza.

Israel will let private sector goods back into Gaza after a Hamas fee dispute stalled commercial shipments. The same week the World Food Programme cut aid to 500,000 Palestinians, citing funding shortages, and the IDF published a Hamas document it says shows plans to plant explosives near camps for displaced people. We break down who controls what enters Gaza and why the fee fight matters.

A Hamas fee dispute stalled Gaza's commercial shipments, and Israel is now resuming the flow of private sector goods anyway. Add the IDF's published Hamas document on explosives near camps for displaced people and the World Food Programme's aid cuts, and the picture of who is squeezing Gaza gets clearer. We lay out the facts and what Hamas's grip means for ordinary Gazans.

Tell me in the chat what you think.
